questions.question: Which of these is a fundamental (base) SI quantity?
questions.explanation:
A fundamental (base) quantity is one that cannot be derived from other quantities. The seven SI base quantities are length, mass, time, electric current, thermodynamic temperature, amount of substance, and luminous intensity. Mass is therefore a base quantity.

• Force is derived (mass × acceleration).
• Energy is derived (force × distance).
• Velocity is derived (displacement / time).

questions.question: Which quantity has the same dimensions as work?
questions.explanation:
Work and energy have the same dimensions: [ML²T⁻²]. Work is the transfer of energy, so they are dimensionally identical.

• Power: [ML²T⁻³]
• Momentum: [MLT⁻¹]
• Force: [MLT⁻²]

questions.question: Which of these is a scalar quantity?
questions.explanation:
A scalar has magnitude only, no direction. Speed is the magnitude of velocity, so it is a scalar.

• Displacement, velocity, and acceleration are vectors (they have direction).

questions.question: Which of these is a vector quantity?
questions.explanation:
A vector has both magnitude and direction. Force is a vector.

• Mass, temperature, and time are scalars.

questions.question: The dot (scalar) product of two vectors gives:
questions.explanation: The dot product (scalar product) of two vectors A·B = |A||B|cos θ yields a scalar. It is used to find the component of one vector along another and to calculate work (F·d).

questions.question: The cross product of two parallel vectors is:
questions.explanation: The cross product magnitude is |A×B| = |A||B|sin θ. For parallel vectors, θ = 0° or 180°, so sin θ = 0, giving the zero vector.

questions.question: The resultant of two vectors is greatest when the angle between them is:
questions.explanation: The magnitude of the resultant is R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ). This is maximum when cos θ = 1, i.e., θ = 0° (vectors point in the same direction).

questions.question: A unit vector has:
questions.explanation: A unit vector is defined as a vector with magnitude exactly 1. It is used to specify direction only. For example, î, ĵ, k̂ are unit vectors along the x, y, and z axes.

questions.question: The rate of change of displacement is:
questions.explanation: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement with respect to time: v = Δs/Δt. Speed is the rate of change of distance; acceleration is the rate of change of velocity; jerk is the rate of change of acceleration.

questions.question: The slope of a velocity–time graph gives:
questions.explanation: The slope of a velocity–time graph is Δv/Δt, which is acceleration. A positive slope means acceleration; a negative slope means deceleration.

questions.question: The area under a velocity–time graph gives:
questions.explanation: The area under a velocity–time graph is the integral of velocity with respect to time, which equals displacement (or distance, depending on sign).

questions.question: A body in free fall near Earth’s surface (ignoring air resistance) has:
questions.explanation: Near Earth's surface, free fall occurs under gravity alone. The acceleration due to gravity g ≈ 9.8 m/s² is essentially constant (ignoring air resistance and altitude changes). So the body has constant acceleration.

questions.question: At the highest point of a projectile’s path, the velocity is:
questions.explanation: At the highest point, the vertical component of velocity is zero (vy = 0), but the horizontal component vx = u cos θ remains unchanged (no horizontal acceleration). So the velocity is horizontal only.

questions.question: The horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are:
questions.explanation: Projectile motion can be analyzed by treating horizontal and vertical motions independently. Horizontally: constant velocity (no acceleration). Vertically: constant acceleration due to gravity. The two motions combine to give the parabolic path.

questions.question: For a given launch speed on level ground, the range is greatest at a launch angle of:
questions.explanation: Range R = (u² sin 2θ)/g. This is maximum when sin 2θ = 1, i.e., 2θ = 90°, so θ = 45°.

questions.question: A body moving at constant speed can still accelerate if:
questions.explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity (a vector). Even if speed is constant, a change in direction means velocity changes, so the body accelerates. This is exactly what happens in uniform circular motion.

questions.question: Newton’s first law is also known as the law of:
questions.explanation: Newton's first law states that a body remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an external force. This is the law of inertia—the tendency of a body to resist changes in its state of motion.

questions.question: According to Newton, the inertia of a body depends on its:
questions.explanation: Inertia is the resistance to change in motion. It is directly proportional to the mass of the body. A more massive body has greater inertia.

questions.question: Newton’s second law states that net force equals the rate of change of:
questions.explanation: Newton's second law: Fnet = dp/dt, where p = mv is momentum. For constant mass, this reduces to F = ma. So force equals the rate of change of momentum.

questions.question: A person in a lift accelerating upward feels:
questions.explanation: In an upward-accelerating lift, the normal reaction N = m(g + a) > mg. The person feels heavier because the floor pushes up with a greater force.

questions.question: Rocket propulsion is best explained by which of Newton’s laws?
questions.explanation: A rocket expels gas backward at high speed. By Newton's third law, the gas exerts an equal and opposite force on the rocket, propelling it forward.

questions.question: Frictional force acts:
questions.explanation: Friction always acts opposite to the direction of relative motion (or attempted motion) between two surfaces in contact.

questions.question: Limiting friction is directly proportional to the:
questions.explanation: Limiting friction FL = μsN, where N is the normal reaction. It is independent of the contact area (for a given normal reaction) and independent of speed.

questions.question: The coefficient of friction:
questions.explanation: The coefficient of friction μ is the ratio of frictional force to normal reaction: μ = F/N. Since it is a ratio of two forces, it is dimensionless (no units).

questions.question: The SI unit of power is the:
questions.explanation:
Power is the rate of doing work: P = W/t. The SI unit is the watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s.

• Joule is energy.
• Newton is force.
• Hertz is frequency.

questions.question: The kinetic energy of a body depends on its:
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy K = ½mv². It depends on both mass and speed (specifically, the square of speed).

questions.question: The work–energy theorem states that net work done equals the change in:
questions.explanation: The work–energy theorem: Wnet = ΔK = ½mv² − ½mu². The net work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy.

questions.question: Which of these is a conservative force?
questions.explanation:
A conservative force is one for which the work done is independent of the path taken and depends only on initial and final positions. Gravity is conservative.

Friction, air resistance, and viscous drag are non-conservative (work depends on path; energy is dissipated as heat).

questions.question: Under conservative forces only, total mechanical energy is:
questions.explanation: The law of conservation of mechanical energy: if only conservative forces act, the total mechanical energy (KE + PE) remains constant.

questions.question: Gravitational potential energy depends on a body’s:
questions.explanation: Gravitational potential energy PE = mgh depends on position (height h) relative to a reference level, as well as mass and g.

questions.question: Linear momentum is the product of:
questions.explanation: Linear momentum p = mv, the product of mass and velocity. It is a vector quantity.

questions.question: Impulse is equal to the change in:
questions.explanation: Impulse J = FΔt. By Newton's second law, F = dp/dt, so J = Δp. Thus impulse equals the change in momentum.

questions.question: In a perfectly elastic collision:
questions.explanation: In a perfectly elastic collision, both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. The bodies bounce apart with no loss of kinetic energy.

questions.question: In uniform circular motion, the centripetal force is directed:
questions.explanation: The centripetal force is always directed towards the centre of the circular path. It is responsible for changing the direction of velocity without changing its magnitude.

questions.question: Which quantity stays constant in uniform circular motion?
questions.explanation: In uniform circular motion, the speed (magnitude of velocity) is constant. Velocity, acceleration, and momentum change direction continuously.

questions.question: The gravitational force between two masses is:
questions.explanation: Gravitation is always attractive. Unlike electric forces (which can be attractive or repulsive), gravity always pulls masses together.

questions.question: Torque is best described as the:
questions.explanation: Torque (τ) is the turning effect of a force about an axis. It is given by τ = rF sin θ, where r is the distance from the axis to the point of application of the force.

questions.question: In simple harmonic motion, the acceleration is directed:
questions.explanation: In SHM, the restoring force (and hence acceleration) is always directed towards the equilibrium position and is proportional to the displacement: a = −ω²x.

questions.question: The period of an oscillation is the:
questions.explanation: The period (T) is the time taken for one complete oscillation (one full cycle). It is the reciprocal of frequency: T = 1/f.

questions.question: In simple harmonic motion, the speed is greatest at the:
questions.explanation: In SHM, speed is maximum at the mean (equilibrium) position where displacement is zero. At the extreme positions, the speed is zero (the body momentarily stops before reversing).
